utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we commence with the witness, in the first place, I'd like to apologise for the Chamber's late arrival. It was due to the fact that we had to meet to consider matters in respect of which I will now give a ruling. The first is the Prosecution request that their investigator be allowed to view the proceedings with an audiovisual aid. The general principle is, of course, that a witness should not be present in court prior to giving evidence, and Rule 90(D) is very practical and it provides that: "A witness who had heard the testimony of another witness shall not for that reason alone be disqualified from testifying." The Chamber fully understands and accepts that principle. The reason given by the Prosecutor for the investigator's presence is, it seems, among other things, to assist the Prosecutor in the preparation of his closing brief. In considering this matter, the Chamber has had to take account of the fact that as a matter of practice, even if it is not a matter of right, the Defence is not allowed to have their investigator present in court. It appears that the basis for this is financial and economic consideration. To have the Prosecutor's investigator in court in a situation in which Defence would not be able, for whatever reason, to have their investigator in court, what it seems to us is a breach of the principle of equality of arms. In those circumstances and for those reasons, the Chamber will not accede to the Prosecutor's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [redacted]. Apparently, this person has written a book, and he believes that he has evidence relevant to these proceedings. While the Chamber does not rule out of the possibility of this person being called as a witness at a later stage in the proceedings, we do not consider it appropriate at this stage to consider the matter of intervening him in these proceedings. So the ruling on that matter is that this is something which should be taken up at a later stage in the proceedings. On the matter of the trial and the progress that is being made in general, I think we are picking up some speed and the pace is improving, but the Chamber would like to see us work towards an objective of dealing with at least one witness in a day -- in a day, and I'd like all parties to bear that in mind and to cooperate in that regard. Yes. We'll continue with the witness. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, let me ask you to try to summarise what we have been saying here yesterday. You said that you had given a statement to the Tribunal investigators, and we determined that there was a statement with your name and your signature for which you said it was not your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said I had given a statement to the Tribunal investigators and that there was a possibility that there was somebody there of whom I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps, on 8th December 1994, meet with a gentleman whose name is Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps give him a written statement on this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there is a possibility that I had given such a statement because I did not know of these persons, but I have already said that when I arrived in Travnik, I gave statements to the authorities there, in what camps I had been and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My understanding of what you said was that you had only given one statement and that was to the Tribunal investigators, so did you give a statement to the authorities in -- of Banja Luka, SJB, on 8 December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I have given a statement to people about what had happened to me on the way to Travnik, but I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Tribunal investigators there at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help me to put this document to the witness, and to -- and to have the witness state without reading any names whether this is indeed his statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the signature and tell me whether this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the only statement you gave that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have already clearly stated that I had given statements to those authorities, where I had been, whom I had seen in these camps and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell us that yesterday? But we have wasted a lot of time trying to determine to whom you spoke and what kind of statements you have given.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had said yesterday, as I am saying today, that I had given statement to the authorities in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you -- why did you say that you stated that that was not your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement that I have given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on that date give another statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher to show the witness this document so that the witness could say whether the document bears his signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please return the documents which I have given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Travnik in 1994, in September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall having said to the Tribunal investigator who had come and talked to you in January of 1995, the first thing that you said, "I have given three statements about the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. It was in November and December, 1994"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a possibility that I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you yesterday and today say different things to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the Chamber would like you to move on. We believe that you have explored the question of statements. We think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I completely accept what you said, and I would like to distribute one copy of each of the statements in Bosnian and English, and we will provide the French versions as soon as possible. And Mr. Greaves has tendered three out of five statements. I would like to tender the remaining two statements so that we have all of them, and I'm sure that my friends of the Prosecution already have copies of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Registrar will give them the appropriate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the kind cooperation of the Prosecution, sufficient numbers of copies were made in Bosnian and English languages, five copies each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... proceedings. I'll ask the Registrar to deal with the question of the numbering and the distribution of the exhibits at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course, we will need to know what the numbers are so that when the next exhibit is tendered, we have the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender another exhibit, the next one, which is the document bearing signature -- a signature of this witness. The original is already with the Registry, and I have sufficient numbers of copies for everybody concerned, and I would like to tender it and have them distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, yesterday you gave evidence about Trnopolje, where you went into some detail. And let me please ask you to please wait for me to finish asking you a question before you give your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So yesterday you said that you were moving down your street in the direction of Keraterm camp. Can you tell me precisely how many people were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, up to 30 people were killed on that day, the 9th Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you -- why did you yesterday say on two occasions, both in examination-in-chief and cross-examination that it was exactly 26 persons who were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 26 persons from my street, which was about one kilometre long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does the number of 30 refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, when we came down to the Omarska-Prijedor road, when we arrived there, there were men from other hamlets, Elezi, Durraci, and Mrakovici, and there were some people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I know that up to 30 people were killed before we arrived in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving the statement to the investigators of this Tribunal, you said on that occasion, exactly 36 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible. It was Durraci Matrici, and I know that 20 people from my street, as I pointed out, were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say to the Prosecutor that there were 36?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-six. As I said, it was a man from Durraci, Matrici, Elezovi, and I didn't know them that well. And the exact figure of 26 I knew because these were men from my street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the investigator that a group of five or six soldiers killed 35 men in front of Mevludin Sejmenovic's and Redzib's house, Esad Redzic's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, 35, and 26 were from my street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were these people killed exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed in front of Esad Redzic, the other men, and the Mevludin's Sejmenovic house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say in the statement of 3rd November to the Bosnian authority that it was 32 Bosniaks who were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say even now that I cannot give you the exact number. Maybe it was up to 50 men who were killed, but I know that from my street it was exactly 26 who were killed. Because at that time, I could not witness every murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a count of those killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a column, and from the column I could see that 26 men were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you then mention these other figures if you did not know the men, if you don't know the exact numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there was about ten bodies on one heap, in one group, and I could not see exactly how many. Maybe there were even more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you make it easier for all of us and say that you did not know how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my street, it was exactly 26 men who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where these men were buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were buried in front of Mevludin Sejmenovic house and Esad and Mevla Redzics' houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were buried in front of Mevla Redzic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 17 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said you were forced to sing Chetnik songs as you were going along that road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did sing Serbian songs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you sang a Halid Muslimovic song.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Halid Muslimovic ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this song a Chetnik one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say Chetnik song. I'm saying -- I'm repeating this again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses there were where you got on in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four or five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which bus were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the first one. When we were coming to the Keraterm camp, I was on the first bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did those buses which brought you stop at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stopped outside the entrance, outside the very entrance, outside the gate where the reception desk was, one after the other, in a column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they stop inside the compound of Keraterm or outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were coming in -- it depends. The first bus came through immediately, and the others behind him had to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the bus went inside the compound of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that precisely, but I think -- I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to show you the Prosecution Exhibit number 2, namely, picture number -- picture A. Please look at the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to put the photograph on the ELMO so we can see what the witness is pointing. [In English] Please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you exactly at that moment when you arrived? Please show us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance to Keraterm from the main road, Prijedor-Banja Luka, which means that if this is the gate into Keraterm, the buses were coming from Banja Luka, Kozarac, and they stopped at the gate. As we were coming in, the first bus had to go through the gate, and up to the reception area, and the others had to stop. Here you see the reception area very clearly. I was beaten up when I was getting off the bus. I reached the reception desk. It could have been a distance of about ten metres. So if the buses came together, the first one could have been inside the compound already, the bus that I was on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this gate which you see, were there any guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I couldn't see that in the evening from the bus. It was night-time. But at the reception hut, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, does it mean that the bus came into this area behind this mobile white gate, the rail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where on this photograph? Perhaps we can't see it. But at the time when you were brought into Keraterm, where was this pile of dirt, the waste pile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reception hut, hall number 1 and 2. That evening I couldn't have known that. All I saw was the reception hut. And later, as I said, a big garbage dump was here by the reception hut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the right, at the rightmost side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reception hut, hall number 1 and 2. This is some sort of warehouse, Rooms 3 or 4, and waste containers, garbage containers. That evening I couldn't have seen that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you then say to the investigators of the OTP the following: "The buses parked next to a garbage dump right inside the compound"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses parked near the hillock. Maybe it was mistranslated. That is the area near the reception hut where I was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing to you -- put my questions precisely, and I would like precise answers. So you told the Office of the Prosecutor that the buses had parked next to the garbage dump. Why did you say that when you are claiming a completely different thing today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this garbage dump, it's possible that I said it. But it was night-time; I couldn't see it. I just said precisely where I was taken off the bus. I was beaten up. I reached the reception hut where I was met by guards who took away my personal documents, some little -- the little valuables that I had. They beat me up. Then they took me towards the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about this. I'm asking you where the buses were and why you said they parked next to the garbage dump when you are showing us now that it's at least 100 metres away from the place where you were brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that this garbage dump was somewhere near the gate, and that I saw it. I clearly showed to you where I got off the bus and where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the witness has offered an explanation. It's a matter now for the Chamber to assess that evidence. Let's move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that at the reception desk by this small hut we see on the picture, that your documents were taken away there but you were not beaten up, not by the reception hut, when you were -- when your documents were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got off the bus, I got beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems to me my questions are fairly precise. Please give me precise answers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was beaten there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say to the Prosecutor then the following: "The next stop was the reception desk where we had to turn over all our personal belongings and where we were beaten again"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please wait for my question to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said where we had to turn over our personal belongings and where we were beaten. I never said that I personally was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just now that you were beaten there and when one says "we," that implies you personally. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the majority of the people who were there. And as for me personally, I'm stating this precisely, I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were grabbed by four soldiers after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the usher. We won't need this photograph any longer. We can continue without it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were grabbed by four soldiers. Where on your body did they -- where did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four soldiers were standing behind that reception desk, perhaps five or ten metres away, and they told me to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make this short, where did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hit me in my chest, where I had haematoma, with their rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there in the room where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, I didn't -- I couldn't have had a complete picture, but it may have been up to 600 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever know the exact number of people who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once, from that monitor of the room, Fehim Grubic -- Krupic, sorry -- I heard that there were 62 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you distinguish between military and police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does each of them look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time of the conflict, there were camouflage and police uniforms around during my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the colours are blue and green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, did you tell us yesterday that one out of the men who interrogated you wore civilian clothes, while two wore military camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One wore civilian clothes, one a military uniform, and Mr. Drljaca wore this camouflage blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see there is a discrepancy between those two statements? You are now speaking about three different uniforms, and yesterday, at 11.41 you said one wore civilian clothes and two wore military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, those were military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me briefly how were you beaten during interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was climbing upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He described this in detail in his evidence in chief. We don't need to go over it all again, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your interrogation, did you notice any motions, movements, made by those people who were interrogating you, Simo Drljaca and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly, when I got in, I sat on that chair that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting to you a precise question. Did you notice anything unusual, any movements with their hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was walking to and fro, that he was making signs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of signs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't possibly know that. Maybe he was walking about, waving his hands. Maybe that's the kind of things he does. Maybe he was signing with his eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you tell to the investigators of the Bosnian authorities that the people who were interrogating you had some signals and motions which served for them to sign when you were -- they were supposed to beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already I was not beaten up like the others were, other people who came broken after beatings. I said clearly about myself that I was hit, punched off a chair, I was asked about my father, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, are you telling us here what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or you are telling us about things that you heard, overheard, or what seems to you had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you indicating clearly when you are speaking about things that you know personally as opposed to things that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I emphasise what I know personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about signals and motions which you noticed, judging by your statement in paragraph number 2, page 5, to the Bosnian government, to the effect that they had some signals and motions to agree on when they were supposed to beat you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got into that room, they fixed me with their eyes. Nobody asked anything. Then one of them got up, walked about, and made a sign with his hands or with his eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did it mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that somebody should beat me up or maybe that the interrogation was over, that I should get out of the room, that the escort who brought me should take me out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noticed that sign. What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: A normal sign. When the interrogation was over, he motioned with his eyes, "Take him out," and the other one took me out without saying a word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they had signals and motions to agree when the beating was supposed to start, not when you were supposed to be taken out. What was the sign for "start beating"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly how I was beaten. I said a man punched me off a chair and kicked me because my father worked in the cultural society of Trnopolje, and he said this brotherhood no longer exists, and I got beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe my questions to this witness are precise. I would like you perhaps to exercise your authority to help me get him to answer my questions precisely. So my question was, what was the signal for "start beating," which he referred to in his statement to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to answer that question? What was the signal that was given for the beating to start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated this clearly. It was a sign made with the eyes or with a hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There you have your answer. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kajin was commander of the camp for a short while and that the reason for his replacement was that he had taken away some prisoners to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there when Kajin took those people away to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, he took away Saban Elezovic, among others. I can't give you exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days after your arrival was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps five or ten days, three. I don't know exactly. All I know is Mr. Kajin took people away and brought them back. In fact, these people did come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it what you said yesterday, "Sometime -- during sometime, briefly while Kajin was commander?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could have been two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that Kajin was soft to the detainees. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that. Maybe that's what I referred to, precisely the fact that those people went to the hospital and came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did Kajin take people to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. I can't know the exact number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I will deal with one subject, Your Honour. I know it has been dealt with before, but this is very important for my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to the Office of the Prosecutor that Kajin replaced Sikirica seven or ten days after your arrival.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I said that, but I think he was commander three or four days after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just a minute ago two to three, now you said three or four. Do you know at all how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, but while I was at the camp, I didn't know even where I was, I was so badly beaten up. I can't give you any dates precisely or measure time, especially not to a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday at a quarter to 3.00, you said, "On the 9th of July, I arrived and Sikirica was already there." You repeated the same thing at 2.47.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was already there, but I didn't say whether he was commander of the camp or not. I stated clearly that after my arrival, Mr. Kajin -- it's possible that I said ten days, but it was three or four days before he was replaced, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be possible that Kajin was commander for two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it possible? Do you allow for that possibility, that he was commander for two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I can't tell you exactly to a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kajin had a girlfriend in Trnopolje. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in his youth. Her name was Josipa Pavlovic, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 nicknamed Lula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday -- you mentioned yesterday a beating of a person named Turkanovic. How many times was this man hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that - he was hit on the head - because he had very bright red hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you tell the Prosecutor precisely that he was hit three times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was hit more times. I didn't count the blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, you knew that it was precisely three times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you saying things you're not sure of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man was killed, and I know that his head was split, and I don't know exactly how many blows there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about this from someone or did you see it personally? Where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, it happened between halls 2 and 3, where bread was cut, towards the toilet in the corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did this man have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely what kind of injuries? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: His head was fractured. His skull had cracked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some on his body. I told you about what I knew. Maybe his arms were broken as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that he had injuries on his neck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I say "head," I think it implies the neck too. It's the upper part of the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those terrible matters we are discussing, it seems that those details are completely indifferent to you. You are saying roughly what occurs to you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not indifferent to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was beaten up. I know how it felt. But I don't know about exact dates, when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding Fikret Avdic, where was this man beaten up exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was called out, taken out of the hall. It was night. I think he was taken away to that room which was by Rooms number 3 or 4 or somewhere outside. We could hear screaming and crying. He was taken back outside the entrance to the hall. He was thrown on the ground there and the guards pulled him inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think it was on the 17th of August, maybe July, mid of that month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor it was between the 22nd and the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say that exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know then it was on the 17th if you don't know any dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just said, it's possible that it happened on the 17th and 18th, because people were taken away all the time and beaten up. I cannot know the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which shift was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Mr. Kajin's shift while Banovic was still there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request would the counsel and the witness please stop overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I don't know whether you heard. The interpreters are asking you to observe the pause between question and answer, and the same applies to the witness. You must wait until the question has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we had a problem -- I think that the witness just said that this was not during Kajin's shift, if I understood him correctly. This is just when we were having a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Banovic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you conclude that this was Kajin's shift because Banovic was there or because Kajin was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that Kajin was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say yesterday that this was during Kajin's shift, and today, you're saying that you're not sure of that at all? Do you know what the consequences are of what you're telling us here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated clearly now that Banovic was there. And you asked me whether this was Kajin's shift and I said yes, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you did not see Kajin on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when we talked about the victim called Saban Elezovic, when referring to that man, you said as follows, "I don't know exactly when he was killed, whether it was in Kole's, Kajin's, or Fustar's shift. I know it was the Banovics." Does that mean that the Banovics could come at any time to beat, mistreat, abuse, regardless of whose shift it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could come into camp when they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I can't help but notice this: That the witness was an hour and a quarter in chief; Mr. Greaves cross-examined for a little over an hour; and you have been cross-examining now for a little over an hour too, an hour and ten minutes. There comes a time when too much time is taken up and can be wasted in cross-examination. We do have to get on with this case. So can you bring your cross-examination as speedily as possible to a close?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best to speed it up. What I'm trying to do is also secure the cooperation of the witness, who I believe is answering things in a way that is too lengthy, and I will try to -- what I will try to do is to reduce most of the questions that I had prepared, following your instruction. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you said, Banovics would come whenever they wanted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were Fikret's injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, he had a small injury on his head but he had internal injuries. He was like broken up. If he drank water, he would throw it up and then something yellow came out. And the next morning, he died in hall number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you placed him on a blanket and carried him out of Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the entrance of Room 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he died in front of the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not tell us yesterday that he died in your arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not die in my arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you in your statement to the Bosnian authority on page 3 say, "He was all broken up and died in my arms"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was in reference to the blanket in which we carried him out. That is practically in my arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a person named Saban Elezovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this person killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that it was yesterday that you said that this man was killed for the first time, when you -- and when you gave four statements to the Prosecution, including a statement on the 13th of March, when you talked to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you consider it important that in the statement that you gave in 1995, in conversation -- and in -- to mention that in your conversation with Mr. Mundis several days ago, that this man was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As here, I was answering questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us all here that it is possible that a professional person who was questioning you did not ask you whether this man was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that man was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that he had injuries on his arm, that the arm was in a cast, and that Cupo had hit him on -- kept hitting him on the right shoulder until it broke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he succumb to those injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, Mr. Kajin took him to the hospital. I don't know when he came back. Later on, he was taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not say so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say how this man was killed, and that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that no one of the persons who interviewed you did not hear what you -- when you said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that I did mention that this man Elezovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A person named Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated clearly, this was Cupo, that this man was lagging behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, don't go so wide. Just who beat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cupo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why in your statement to the Prosecution in 1995 you said that it was Faca who beat him and you never mentioned Cupo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Faca was also a steady visitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Faca hit him or do you just know that Faca was a steady visitor so, for anything that happened, perhaps it was Faca, it was Banovic or it was Kondic, or do you actually know precisely who hit whom when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Faca was there and Banovic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also mentioned Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he too was coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Duca at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of injuries did Mesic have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Zigic shot the roof of the hall, whom did he hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: He hit a man, I think that his last name was Jakupovic, I'm not sure. This bullet hit him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say to the AID - to the Bosnian authorities, that is; let me correct myself here - that this man Hodzic was from Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having said that, because among all those men, I could not know all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day after the Room 3 massacre, you said that that morning you were let outside to go to the toilet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you came out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that night -- let me ask, are you referring to the day after the massacre?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw dead men in front of the room, because I had to run to the toilet and come back quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not count them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been five or six bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw Kajin that morning. The question is simple: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that he had come and said that there had been a massacre and that he had asked whether there was someone who would volunteer with -- to help, and that he did not force anyone to do anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were killed exactly on that day -- that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, two men came out of my hall who loaded up these bodies, and they said that perhaps there were up -- up to 200 casualties, 160 to 200, with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you say to the Prosecutor that there were exactly 186?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but I stated clearly that I had heard from the men who had loaded them and that that number does not mean that it is an accurate number, because I did not load these bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you count those people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the people who went to load them up did count them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why are you telling us -- whenever we ask you, you give us different numbers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated clearly that in front of Room 3, I saw five or six bodies when I was running to the toilet. I did not load up the bodies, and in my statement, I had heard from -- I said that I had -- from these men who were loading, Hazim Sivac, Hadjo Sivac that whether this number is correct or not, that I am in no position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it's clear that his testimony in this matter is based on what was told to him and it's an estimate. So I wouldn't pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm moving on, Your Honour. I agree with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men killed by Faca, can you tell me how that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very entrance to hall 2, to the left of the door there was a barrel where we relieved ourselves. That night, this man was on the barrel, and Faca came and from a distance, one, two, or three metres, said something like, "Hey policeman from Kozarac," or, "You from Brdo," and then he shot him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did he fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he fired once, one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he hit him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was night-time, but he hit him in the chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was night-time. Does that mean that you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see it because it was three to four metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you point out that it was night-time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that it was night-time, but the distance was two or three metres from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Sakib Sivac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by sight. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the room where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The men from Sivci and Trnopolje were in that room, so he could have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you conclude on the basis of the fact that people from the village of Sivci were there that the person with the name Sivac was also there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, "I think it was Kajin's shift." Does that again mean that you're not sure that it was Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when people were taken away?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm meaning -- I mean the killing of the man on the barrel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was killed by Faca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not sure that it was in Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I wasn't sure, but I know that Faca killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're sure that it was not -- you're not sure that it was in Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it perhaps yes or perhaps no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: You clearly asked me whether Faca killed that man. I said yes. And I cannot know whether this was Kajin's shift or not, not now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this happened after the massacre. To the Prosecutor, you said that it happened one night after the massacre in Room 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why in the statement to the Bosnian authorities you said that this was the same night when Sikirica killed a man and that that was one night before the massacre in Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly that I am -- I cannot know when I was beaten up, but I know that this man was killed one night before or after. I don't know if that means something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you that it is meaningless in light of the fact that this was a tragic occurrence, but it is important for this Trial Chamber to determine as accurately as possible when some of these happened, and this is why I'm asking you these questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you will be finishing before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best to do that. I only have three or four questions, and I beg for your indulgence and patience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the situation when you were mistreated. Yesterday, you said that when Banovic beat you that he broke your nose.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That the front tooth in the upper jaw was broken and that I still have scars from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript from yesterday, it says that your nose was broken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a front tooth. You can still see that. And there are scars too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that you had understood that Banovic wanted to stab you in the chest and that you raised your arms to protect yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, instinctively. My left arm against my chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say to the Bosnian authorities that you instinctively raised your arms to protect your head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is logical. Your arms are moving upwards towards your head to protect yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Kajin arrive, before Banovic stabbed you or after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajin arrived at the gate on some small motorcycle. I don't know what the reason was. He had not yet entered the perimeter. I don't know whether Banovic became scared or something, but when he saw Kajin arriving, he tried to stab me, and he cut my arm, and he said, "Go back to the hall."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- in your statement to the Prosecutor, you said that Kajin saved you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that his arrival saved my life. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question in respect of a man called Emsud Bahonjic. Are you quite sure that you personally were present at the time when this man lost his life in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you personally saw that this man was beaten up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there are persons -- that there is evidence that this man died more than 20 days before your arrival in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times was he beaten; Mr. Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say to the Prosecutor that he was beaten five times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. As I said before, I can say accurately when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at the time the commander of the guard was Kajin. How do you know that Kajin was commander of the guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said when I arrived in the camp, and I don't know how many days, Mr. Kajin was commander and then he was relieved of duty. In my opinion, because he was taking people to the hospital and bringing them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that on one of the nights when Emsud was beaten Kajin was the commander of the guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because men from Kajin's shift were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Banovics, of the ones that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you told us that the Banovics came all the time regardless of the shifts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you know, then, that that night they did not come in outside of their shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was their regular shift, but they could come in whenever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how do you know that that night, when Emsud Bahonjic was beaten, it was Kajin's shift, if Banovics were able to come to any other shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was exactly that shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the basis of your -- of that memory that you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the two twin brothers -- the two twin brothers were on the same shift, and I know that it was Kajin's shift. They could come whenever they wanted. One was at the reception hut and the other one was at the guard point that was to the left of the hut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was how do you know that that evening it was Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Kajin's shift was on because they were at their guard points. Otherwise, they would just come to the camp, and they would bring people out and beat them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that Cupo was beating, that is one of the Banovics, Duca and Zigic. All I can conclude from that was that they were not on their guard duty but that they were involved in a beating.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did see them on their guard posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where did you see that they were on their guard posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my room, number 2, is in front of this reception hut, and from the door - and it wasn't a door, it was the bars - you could see. I could see precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that is what I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Adnan Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Adnan Bahonjic. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, in a statement that he gave to the Tribunal investigators, says as follows: "On 7, 8, and 9 June, four men were brought to the camp. Among them was my cousin, Emsud Bahonjic, born 1962. He was taken to Room number 2." Then he says -- he mentions Emsud going to the hospital, and he was only looked at there and brought back. "Two to four days after he was brought back from the hospital, Emsud passed away." Do you have any comment to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Emsud was in the camp while I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there is evidence that Emsud Bahonjic was taken to the hospital on the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Inaudible] ... that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am putting it to you, sir, that you were not at the Keraterm camp at the time when Emsud Bahonjic was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We are very near to the break, so we will take the break now and Mr. Vucicevic will then cross-examine. Witness H, we will take a break until 11.30. During the break, you are reminded that you are not to discuss your evidence with anyone, and that includes members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic. [B/C/S translation on English channel]. I neglected to say the registrar the exhibits produced by Mr. Petrovic -- [B/C/S translation on English channel]. We are hearing B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the B/C/S is switched from channel 6 to channel 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we now all right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement of the 15th and 16th of January, 1995 will be numbered Defence Exhibit 3/2; witness statement date 3rd of November, 1994, Defence Exhibit D4/2; the witness statement number 023/2, dated 8 December 1994, will be Defence Exhibit D5/2; witness statement number 023/3, date 8 December 1994, will be Defence Exhibit D6/2; undated witness statement, in the right upper corner the number 00685203 on the English version will be Defence Exhibit D7/2; the paper containing five signatures of Witness H will be Defence Exhibit D8/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [redacted]. This is a proffer that was prepared by an investigator in the Office of the Prosecutor, and I don't believe there's been any evidence that this witness has even been shown this document or if it was ever read back to him in B/C/S or that he's ever affirmed it in any other way, so we would have an objection with respect to the proffer without any evidentiary foundation that this witness has ever seen this document, and again, it's D7/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll deal with the point that you have raised, Mr. Mundis, at a later stage. Mr. Vucicevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Vucicevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, my name is Dusan Vucicevic. I am a lawyer from Chicago, and I represent Dragan Kolundzija. I know that you have testified for a long time, and you said this morning, "I know that I was beaten up, but I don't know the exact days when I was beaten up." However - and this is my question - since almost nine years went by and it's difficult for you to remember even when you were beaten up, it may be probable -- it may be possible that you don't remember about many other facts. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please. Did not hear the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About any answer where you're not sure, please say so, because anything else you might say is superfluous, and if we continue this way, your testimony here will finish within 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the answer on the previous question that the witness stated he was beaten by Banovics did not enter the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you'd just like to reaffirm your previous answer. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was beaten up by the Banovics. I was beaten by Cupo Banovic. I know that date. That was on the 30th of July. And I was taken out on other occasions; I don't know the exact dates. That's what I said yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you also don't remember how many times you were beaten because, if you did remember, you would have told us by now in your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten during interrogation and upon arrival, on the 30th, that I remember, and one other time. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to tell the Court where you have worked and on what jobs you did since you left the army? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly that I was attached to the army. You mean the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Since you completed your regular military service you did in the JNA, what jobs did you do until the 10th of July, 1992? In what enterprises did you work and what jobs you performed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in Riboprodukt Sanicani. I worked in Croatia in enterprise Graditelj. I worked in a Zagreb company, Sigurnost. I also worked in a private enterprise owned by Mirsad Kubic. I worked in a kebab shop. From the very beginning of the war, I worked in Slovenia in Lujbljana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in any other place apart from those you have just enumerated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the military post, Brcko near Zagreb. I worked for many private entrepreneurs who owned cafes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in a socially owned or a state-owned company which you did not mention now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Graditelj from Sisak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other state company in Prijedor, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Riboprodukt of Sanicani. That's what I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never worked in a wheelbarrow factory in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit it, at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were testifying, the Prosecutor asked you this question, and since I quote directly from the transcript, I will read in English. [In English] "Witness, do you recall any of the smells or odours that were in the camp on that evening?" You gave the following answer: "Yes. One could smell something like tear gas. Tear gas was thrown at them, because it has a specific smell and, of course, it itches your eyes and the mucus and the nerves."

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Usher, could you please show the witness the book with the pictures?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness H, will you please show us on the photograph where it is most clearly visible in your opinion where was Room 2 and Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will point it out. But before all this camp --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, this was not the question. Please answer the question because we want to finish this soon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1 and this was Room number 2. The room where bread was distributed. And this, somewhere here, was Room 3, behind number 2. And the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember today, what is the distance between Room number 2 and Room number 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 20, 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could be 40, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Room 3 and Room 4 were adjacent; there was only a partition wall between them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into Room 3 or Room number 4. I cannot say this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. We are done with the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were testifying yesterday in response to the Prosecutor's questions, you didn't tell us how you could tell the smell of tear gas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the smell of tear gas could be felt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please kindly, if you are able, answer directly my questions because all my questions are based on the record, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I smelled tear gas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: In order to be able to tell the smell of tear gas, you must have smelled it before in your life.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you do your regular military service in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Sad and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had served in a firefighting unit. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe what kind of basic training did you have in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my service?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, first of all, we had to go through infantry training, which I did in Novi Sad. It lasted for about three or four months, since I graduated from the firefighting school. For people that did not have that kind of special training, there was a firefighting course lasting about seven days. After that, we were transferred to other towns.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the number of days wasn't clearly heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript, you have indicated that your basic training was 40 days, 4-0, and not seven days, as it was translated. Are you correct -- are we correct on that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty days was the duration of the firefighting course in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after being transferred, you had no further training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did my military service in Belgrade in a firefighting unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you have occasion to smell tear gas in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my infantry training in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was routine infantry training, not firefighting training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, when I came to the JNA, first we went through infantry training as young conscripts. After that, we were assigned depending on how we were recruited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, I beg you to concentrate on my questions and answer my questions only. My question was: During your basic infantry training, did you smell tear gas for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe on which occasion this happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was tactical training when we went out to drill ground. We had -- we were issued with masks. And soldiers, as soldiers do, removed safety catches from these masks, and we could smell tear gas. And when you smell it, it stays with you for a long time, even when this first atomic sensation passes, which sort of irritates your nose, the biting sensation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of your platoon commander during your training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a young man by the name of Bosko, somewhere from Derventa. And the commander of the company was Mr. Simic, commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name, the first name, of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his first name. He came there after being transferred. He wore a blue uniform, not the olive-green/grey one. At this time, this uniform was worn by soldiers who serve at airports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which month of which year did you have these drills on the drill ground when you smelled tear gas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the army on the 6th of January, 1982. It was winter, and my training was during the winter and the spring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that drill ground where you had your training?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, is this going to help the Trial Chamber to go into this sort of detail about events 20 years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed it is going to help because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the Witness B, who was in Room 4, has testified to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made your point. You've made your point. You've cross-examined this witness thoroughly about the experience which he's had. Now, that being so, this is a Chamber of professional Judges. We don't need all this detail about events a very long time ago. Now, let's concentrate on what's relevant. You've made your point with his training.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified -- I'm not arguing with the Court. I just want to explain my line of reasoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can follow your line of reasoning. Now let's get on with events which are pertinent to this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this witness has discredited his testimony about tear gas with his experience, I would respectfully accept your ruling. However, if we are going to bring the witnesses that are going to testify that there was never such a training at such location, we do need information about the witness, about witness' training, experience, and persons who were present. I mean I'm just merely trying to establish foundation for his testimony and bring the other witness who are either going to corroborate or refute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
