utterances.text: You are going to bring witnesses about training in relation to tear gas in the JNA 20 years ago. Is that what you're Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 proposing to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: At the time and the place that the witness is saying that this indeed had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I've heard what you have to say. You have laid a sufficient foundation for you to bring the witnesses, who will testify to the contrary. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were confined in Room number 2 at Keraterm; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when Captain Cirkin was brought into Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I came to the camp on the 9th of July, Captain Cirkin was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from the other inmates from Room number 2 how long Captain Cirkin was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard he had been there, but not in Room number 2, hall number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know whether he was in hall number 1, 2, 3, or 4, because you hadn't been there, you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that while I personally was there, he was not in hall number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony that you presented on direct examination, this question was posed to you, referring to Kole: "Do you recall approximately how many times you may have seen him before you arrived at the camp?" You answered. "It was on a number of occasions in town. But I wasn't close to him. I did not communicate with him. It was all just in passing."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did give that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a sworn statement that you have given to authorised officer of Ministry of the Interior, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on November 3, 1994, you have stated the following: [As read] "Kole is about 35 years old, tall, brown hair /?and eyes/, and he may have worked in Kolska in Prijedor because I used to see him there."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said because Kolska was near the railway station. I said yesterday that I saw him there in Prijedor on the bus stop where those cafes and other catering establishments were, where I -- which I visited regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you testified in direct, you -- the question was: "Do you recall where you may have seen him in passing in town, what types of places you may have seen him?" You answered: "Yes. I did see him in coffee bars and a number of occasions in Prijedor, at railway station and bus station." My question to you now is: What did Kole do for living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you it was my opinion that he worked in Kolska. I heard about it. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, the question was rather simple. What did he do for a living, if you know? If you don't, you just state that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there in passing, in coffee bars. He was drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully ask that the witness be instructed to answer the question. The question was rather direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I think he had in fact attempted to answer it. I think he said he saw him in coffee bars, a number of places in Prijedor, at railway stations and a bus station. Are you able to say, Witness H, what Kole did for a living? If you are not, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not know. I did not know exactly where he worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So there you have the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in a sworn statement that you just said now, that you have indeed made, you said you saw him at Kolska. You didn't say you saw him at the restaurant or a cafe at a railroad station. You didn't say at that time that you saw him in coffee bars. You said you saw him at Kolska, right in the big enterprise which employed many people. You saw him in there. How could you explain the difference, what you said in November of 1994, when your recollection was indeed so fresh, only two years after these events have transpired, and today, nine years, where you are placing him in all other various locations? And if I may remind you, you have been sworn to tell the whole truth, but not partial truth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that I said -- it is possible that he worked at Kolska and not that he did work there. I think this is how it was stated, not that I said seen him in Kolska because it was a very large place. I think that I said that I thought that he had worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have the explanation. It's a matter for us now to assess and determine whether we accept it or not. So please move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in Prijedor, and in many other cities that you were at, that somebody by name Kosta could be called Kole, somebody by named Kostic could be called Kole? Kole is a nickname that people with a similar names are called; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you testified there are so many people that worked in Kolska, so it is highly likely that there was another Kole who worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I said that I saw that man on several occasions around the railway stations, in those bars, so that was that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't that a fact that people who hang about the restaurants and the railroad station in Prijedor and other ones are usually those that were either alcoholics or problematic characters, because those restaurants never closed up? They were open 24 hours; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I see Mr. Mundis rising. That's not a proper question to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has testified he has seen him there and there was testimony that Banovic was identified being there most of the time, and, you know, I just want to find out does he know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you're asking him to say whether people who hang about the restaurants are usually people who are either alcoholics or problematic characters because those restaurants are never closed. Can you say that, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, the people who were there were not really alcoholics. These were people who were travelling, because it was the railway station and these were places that were well-appointed. And the young people also patronised them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in one of those restaurants at Kolska or the railroad station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as I said, I didn't have access to Kolska, and I did not work there. And as far as Cupo Banovic is concerned, I could see him before the war around the express place and maybe even the railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Zigic at the restaurant by the railroad station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic was everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you remember whether you saw him at any time at that particular location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified yesterday that you did not know the name of a gentleman whom you identified here in court before you came to the Keraterm and that you just saw him in passing; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also testified that you have seen him there for the three weeks while you were there, indicating that you could see him on every second day if the doors were open. That is direct quotations from your yesterday's testimony. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it was his shift, because I did not see Mr. Kole coming to the camp unless his shift was on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We certainly agree on that one. However, Kole wasn't there for three weeks for you to see him. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I clearly said that I did not know what the order of shifts was, but every other day. If this is how their shift changed, he would be on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to emphasise is that you don't remember whether Kole was there for three weeks or two weeks during your stay in Keraterm. That you don't remember, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I arrived in the camp on the 9th July, and from that day until the closure of the camp, Kole was there when his shift was on duty. I stated that clearly. He was in the camp. That means that I was able to see him. I could see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After July 24th until the time that Keraterm was disbanded, how many times did you see Kole in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. As I said, I could see him as many times as his -- as the number of shifts that he was on if he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So perhaps from your answer this proposition may be correct, that you, throughout this period of time, from 24th until the August 5th, you haven't seen him one single time. Do you agree with me? Only throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was ten days that we are talking, from 25th through the 5th. And since you stated before that you -- that the shifts were changing, rotating every two days, that follows that you have seen him there five times. Have you seen him there five times in that period of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw Mr. Kole during his shift, and I can't know about all the shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back from the time that you for -- the first time that somebody told you this was Kole. Who was that who told you this was Kole? I only want to know the name, nothing else, if you remember. If you don't, say just you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I say before Their Honours and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we want to move on, as you heard the Court saying for so often. I'm only asking you a direct question and I'm asking for the answer. Who told you this was Kole? If you don't remember, you don't remember. I'll ask the following question. Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the inmates, and I personally met him in front of the reception hut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we'll move on. So neither then nor now, you don't remember the name of the man who said this was Kole, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally met Kole in front of the reception hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I have no more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Any re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but just for clarification, with respect to Defence Exhibits D3/2 through D7/2, we would respectfully request that those be under seal since obviously as statements of the witness they contain information that would identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be so, and we will also be giving consideration to the submissions you made about D7/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness H, that concludes your testimony. You may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Prior to calling the next witness, I want to indicate that we are acutely aware of Your Honours' ruling concerning -- or the suggestion that the Prosecution should carry out a very careful review as to what number of witnesses we would be asking protective measures for. The difficulty with the next witness is that he has given evidence in previous proceedings and did so in open testimony. Circumstances, however, have drastically changed since 1996, when he testified, and the witness has been given a pseudonym in these proceedings, but - sorry. My microphone - but is now -- is now asking for protective measures. We have tried to explain to him the difficulty about the fine balancing act that the Court needs to perform between granting protective measures for certain witnesses under certain circumstances and the requirement for as open a proceeding as possible. The witness insists, however, I'm told, that an application be made for protective measures and, under Rule 75(B), I understand that this Court can ask for an in-camera proceeding in order to canvass the reasons why, in this particular case, the witness ought be granted those protective measures that he is seeking, even though, back in 1996, he did testify in open proceedings. I had canvassed this matter with my friends yesterday, and was led to believe that there would be no objection. This morning, however, I understand that the -- that one of my friends reconsidered the fact that the witness had given evidence in open proceedings in 1996 and accordingly, I understand, does have an objection. I would propose that we call the witness in private session and have him give the reasons to Your Honours as to why it is that he feels that the circumstances have changed whereby the court ought to grant protective measures to him. My concern is that he's indicated to us that if he's not granted protective measures, he may not testify of his own volition. Those are my concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, would you just indicate to us what are the changed circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. My understanding is that, as you are aware, in 1996, there was not the same political climate in Bosnia that allowed people to go back to their homes. In very recent years, there is not only a very strong push for that, but the witnesses and their relatives are in fact returning. This particular witness, I understand, has an elderly father who is going to be returning within a month or two, and the witness himself wants to relocate from a foreign country to -- back to this area, and feels that those circumstances, especially for his family, are such that he does not want his visage, as it were, made known to members of the public who now, since technology and CNN, could be watching this broadcast live in Bosnia and see his face, and the granting of a pseudonym is of absolutely no help to him or his family if they are returning in the immediate future. I believe -- I believe him when he says that he is concerned for his family's safety and does not want to risk or jeopardise the safety of his family members, and of course, he is a significant witness for the Prosecution. Those, I understand, are the changed circumstances, that in 1996, when he didn't seek protective measures, the climate was totally different. These people did not then know that they would be able to go back. Now it's not only they can go back, but they are returning, and their relatives are returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Yes, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me to comment on this proposal. We strongly oppose the protective measures for this witness, and I'll give you the reasons for this. The first thing is that this witness has testified twice, in July 1996 and then again in November of 1996, with his -- he testified without any protective measures, with his full name. At that time, in 1996, the situation in Bosnia, that is true, was very different. It is true that it was different, in the sense that now it is much better. Thousands of people have returned to the Prijedor area. The houses in the Kozarac have been repaired and people have been living in them for now a year or two. We have a drastic change of situation, the change for better. And the situation that we are discussing, I have not heard from my learned friend that the witness, who testified in the Tadic case, had any problems after two testimonies -- two of his testimonies in open court. The second point is that this witness is giving very damaging evidence against our client, evidence that cannot be found in hundreds of other statements that we have been discovered to us, and this is why we believe, because the serious charges that this witness is trying to give before this Trial Chamber, he is trying to hide, he is trying to hide behind his scrambled voice and his concealed identity. It is the first time that he is speaking out about Keraterm, and it raises very serious suspicions in the eyes of the Dosen counsel, that he may have special reasons to want to give testimony under such protective measures. So I would like the Trial Chamber to bear this in mind, as well as the fact that what we have suggested yesterday, that is that the witness should say what he has to say in open court, because he is going to give very serious evidence against our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... proposition from my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecutor. On principle, again, in particular, the situation in Bosnia has changed. However, I would like to remind you what I said in my opening statement, the fear, rational or irrational, was a problem when this conflict started, but as this judicial body is attempting to heal to a degree wounds of those people by finding the truth, giving -- yielding to the tenuous even threats that the witness could withdraw would be perhaps, not on the part of the Trial Chamber or any officers sitting in this court, to countenance somebody's misstatements or allowing somebody to disavow what he has said in the past. We all know that under the cloaks, there are a lot of things that do not smell. And from that point, I would like to refer you at the statute, which grants the accused a right of the public trial. So I respectfully ask you to reject this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Mr. Greaves? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of the accused Sikirica absolutely seconds the positions of my learned colleagues, Petrovic and Vucicevic. We oppose the application of the Prosecution for protective measures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, one matter for clarification and the other matter for something that I didn't mention. My friend suggests that we are asking both for the facial distortion and scrambled voice. That is not the case. Only the facial distortion, nothing to do with the voice. He has, as I understand it, at least at the Pre-Trial phase, been granted a pseudonym, K13. The other issue that I have not mentioned is that in your considerations, and in determining whether or not this is a reasonably held fear or whether or not it is at least a fear that the witness may have for the safety of family members as opposed to for himself, consider the fact that there are still currently indictees at large which may play Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 a large role in the witness' concerns about the safety of family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, has the witness clearly indicated to you that he intends to return?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The last information that I have -- I did not speak to the witness personally, but I have spoken to members of our -- of the Prosecution staff who have spoken to him about that issue, and my understanding -- what I have been told unequivocally is that his father is intending to return very soon, within the next few months, and this witness does intend to return at some future time. I have not been told, nor can I assist the court, with what "at some future time" means. I took it to mean -- well, that would be speculation on my part. I could, if I get a short break, either call the witness for the Court to ask him questions or make some inquiries about that issue, should you require further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the date of the last trial that he testified in?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As I believe Mr. Petrovic indicated, it was 1996. It was the Tadic case. And I believe he was called on -- I have -- actually, I have the dates right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's sufficient information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in for the Chamber to ask some questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And should that be in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, you have a witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I have a witness. Call, please, Ante Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Baly. Examined by Ms. Baly:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Ante Tomic and are you a Croatian by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to move a bit closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, would you come closer to the microphone, please. Bring your chair forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were you born on the 1st of January, 1958, and did you -- prior to the war, did you live in the town of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that Ljubija had a population of about 12.000 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 people?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The town of Ljubija is located just outside Ljubija proper, on the road to Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. In particular, did you live in Donji Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No. In Gornji Ljubija or Upper Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that Ljubija, that is prior to the war, had, roughly speaking, a population that was 50 per cent Croatian, 30 per cent Muslim, and 20 per cent Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that the villages surrounding Ljubija were entirely Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, in 1976, after you received a diploma from Ljubija high school, did you attend a period of compulsory military service in the JNA and was that in 1981?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you deployed for a period of time in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that about a one-year period?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in 1983, did you return to Prijedor and commence employment in a workshop in Prijedor and then the following year commence a job with the Omarska mines?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in that position until the start of the war, that is, in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, did you receive four mobilisation summonses?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the case, Mr. Tomic, that you didn't respond to those summonses?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That is correct, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: One was supposed to go to some -- to a war which for me -- in fact, against which I was, against that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your particular reserve unit, was that -- were you told where your particular reserve unit was going to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that it was to be for the defence of Bosnia, that they would be deployed on the borders of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that in fact what took place, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I know that that isn't exactly what happened. My unit went to the front in Croatia, mostly Lipik and Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case, Mr. Tomic, that you supported the reformist party of Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the last election in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I voted for the reformist party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain briefly to the court what the political platform of that party was?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Everything was based on the economy. It was less a political, a more economic-based party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that it didn't fare very well in the elections that were held in 1991, or possibly in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from what I knew, they only won in Tuzla, and otherwise they fared fairly poorly in the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I take you, please, to April the 30th, 1992? On that day, was the municipality of Prijedor taken over by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of April, the SDS party took over the power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Ljubija that day? And if so, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That evening, I was in a coffee bar, and around 10.00 a -- police officers came in and said that we should leave and that the place should close, that there was a curfew. These were -- this is the first knowledge I had about the change of power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the case that the curfew was to be observed after 10.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also notice that there were a lot of troops in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Not more than the usual numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything at that time about the situation with regard to weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Because there were these non-stop mobilisations going on, people were coming back from the front. They brought weapons with them. The weapons were distributed to particular groups of people. Many were armed. Weapons were to be found all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which particular groups received these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Weapons were received by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any heavy weapons in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Specifically in Ljubija, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in the villages surrounding Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In this period, people didn't dare go out, so I don't know what was going on in the villages except from what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've given some evidence that a curfew was imposed and that curfew was to be observed after 10.00. Did you in fact observe the curfew?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any demonstrations against that curfew?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every night, we organised ourselves and we would organise walks or strolls that took place for 30 or 45 minutes, until we would be dispersed by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that organised and participated in these walks, and was there any political connection of any political party involved in the walks?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: There was no party involved. We did it spontaneously. Every night the same people showed up, young women from Ljubija, and we socialised. It was people from this cafe, and we would start from this cafe where we usually gathered, and we would start walking about and there would be 20 or 30 of us involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention towards the structure of the police force in Ljubija. What, prior to the takeover, roughly speaking, was the structure insofar as the ethnicity of the policemen was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I had not much contact with the police, but -- but the police that was in place before the takeover of power went on. In other words, there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs. The commander was an ethnic Croat, Branko Bjekic, and he remain the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the Territorial Defence and what was taking place in that respect at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I did not know anything special about them. I knew that they were there, that they were stationed in the former secondary school in Ljubija. It was a technical school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, on the 24th of May, 1992, did you attend your workplace, that is, at Omarska mines, and did you attend there on an ordinary bus?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, except we did not take the usual route that we used to take every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Prijedor by the usual route, but we took a roundabout way to come back because we had heard that there were some protests or demonstrations going on in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- that evening when you returned home, did you become aware of a shooting that had taken place in the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: On the way back from Omarska, first of all, they didn't let us through. They didn't let the bus through to go to Ljubija. They wanted us to go back because allegedly there was shooting at Hambarine. That was between Ljubija and Prijedor. But the driver took us to Ljubija using an alternate route. And then we later heard that there was an exchange of fire between the Territorial Defence that was on the road below Hambarine and the Serb soldiers. This is what we learned that evening, that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually arrive in Ljubija safely?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, with some stoppages, but we arrived safely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think that evening you were visited by -- by a man who indicated that the army seemed ready to attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He didn't come to me. I was again in the same coffee bar that night, and a man from Donja Ljubija came in and said that the military was on the move and they were preparing to attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- what did you do in response to finding out that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: With several other friends, we prepared ourselves. I put on my military uniform, and we went to -- in the direction of Donja Ljubija. Halfway on the way, we were stopped by members of the Territorial Defence and barred us from continuing on our way and took us to that school building. Then the sirens sounded so that we stayed in that school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this school building was in Ljubija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I take you to around the middle of June? At that time were you still in Ljubija and did something happen to you? And if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically, nothing special was happening except that one could not leave Ljubija. The phone lines outside were all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 severed. We had no communications with Prijedor. You couldn't go anywhere. Buses were not running. We were completely isolated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime toward the middle of June, in the night, did something specifically happen to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the night of 13 and 14 June, I was arrested by the Serb soldiers and that happened in my apartment in -- at my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who these Serb soldiers were? And if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: These were my first-door neighbours, two of them. Two of them came to the apartment, Radenko Djuric, and I cannot remember the other one's name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I was taken out of my apartment and there was a van waiting. There were another 12 people there who had been detained the same night. And at first, they took us to the Rudar soccer stadium. They kept us there for about one hour. And then they all put us in the -- in this van again and took us to Prijedor. That is to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, those other prisoners in the van, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they appear to you? Did they appear to be in good health to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, they did except for one who had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: And he was barefoot. One of them had his pyjamas on. But except for one, the others were all in good health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to your arrival at the Keraterm camp, is it the case that you remained in Keraterm until the 4th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that day, were you transferred to the Omarska Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you know who the person was -- or who was involved in organising the arrest of the non-Serbs from your area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: There were several people who were arresting and demanding -- detaining people and others who compiled lists of people for certain camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone was in charge of that process, and if so, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I know people who were leading that Ljubija staff, and they were probably responsible for that, for the lists, for arrests, for detaining people. They were all my --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection to this latest testimony. I believe that Ms. Baly could develop the foundation, if he had known those men, who they were, how did they get it. It is not the matter how it's presented, but basically whether the witness had known all those details that make his foundation credible, that make his testimony credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for the witness to say whether he knew anyone who was in charge of the process, and if so, who was that person. Are you able to say precisely? Do you know who was in charge of the process?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I know who was the main person in the Crisis Staff in Ljubija. That was a man named Taranjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were you present and did you see new prisoners arriving at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. New prisoners were arriving daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any particular person who would bring those prisoners to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Most often, most frequently, it was Milan Curguz called Krivi who was bringing them but other policemen from Ljubija also brought prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it the case that you actually arrived at Keraterm very early one morning at about 5.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that from this point on, I think that we should refrain from leading questions because we're coming to an area that is directly relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems, Ms. Baly, that we're approaching controversial matters, so no more leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time, Mr. Tomic, did you arrive at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: We arrived at Keraterm early in the morning, about 5.00, 5.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly, please, what happened upon your arrival at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: We arrived in front of the entrance to the camp. We got off the van, and we had our names taken down, and then they were let into the camp and brought in front of the factory with the plant of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you detained in any particular room while you were at Keraterm camp, and if so, what room was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Nobody assigned us to any room. We were just left there. And this group which I was did not find room, and we went to Room 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Room 2 for the entire period in which you were detained at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No. The first day we spent in Room 2, and in the evening, we were transferred to Room 4. And I moved back and forth several times between Rooms 2 and 4, back and forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you do that and how were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That first night we spent in Room 4. By the next day, we decided to move back to Room 2 because we felt that it was safer to be in a room where more people were staying, because we felt that it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were there other persons from Ljubija detained at Keraterm, and if so, can you indicate to the Court how many?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: This first group that arrived 13th to 14th June, we met up with two other local Ljubija men who had been captured previously in Prijedor, and after that, daily new arrivals were coming in, so that in the end we were 115.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know there was 115 from Ljubija there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Because one day before we were to leave Keraterm, a list was compiled with 115 men from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were you involved in compiling any other lists of detainees while you were at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion while I was in Room 2, one of the prisoners, Milan Anusic, called Nono, got a notebook and an order to take down the names of all those who were in this room. He wrote down 250 names, and he asked me to finish off the list, and I did the job, and the last number entered was 396.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did he receive this order and where did he get the notebook?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Both the notebook and the order came from Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this list?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Anusic kept a list throughout that period, and if needed, if the shift leader asked for someone -- was asking for someone, they would use that notebook. People would move from room to room to hide, so they would go around using these lists to try to find people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what eventually happened to that list?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: After about three weeks, we left Keraterm and the list remained in Keraterm. I don't know with whom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to a person, Kajin. What position did that person occupy in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: From what I know, Kajin was one of the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many shift leaders were there and can you name them, the others, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: While I was there, I knew of Kajin, Tomo, Kole. I don't know what Sikirica was, but that name also featured. I don't know if he specifically was also there or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to Kajin, do you know the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time. Only Kajin. That is how everybody referred to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Kajin prior to your detention in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able now, please, to describe to the court what that person Kajin looked like, both in terms of his physical body and the clothing that he wore in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Kajin was about 24, 25 years old. He was quite tall. He was perhaps 185, 190 centimetres tall. I don't know what else to say. We did not have much contact. I saw him on a daily basis but, as I said, I had not known him before, and the only contacts we had were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What clothing did he wear when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that he was wearing a blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know, Mr. Tomic, that he was a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: By his behaviour and also by the fact that the keys to the rooms in which we were locked were -- would be carried around by him. He would open and lock and unlock these doors, and he would order other guards to do it. And by the stories of other inmates who had already been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, if you were to see this person Kajin today, do you think you'd be able to recognise him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I would recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I take you back and ask you to focus again on the first day that you arrived in the camp? And just indicate what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That day, after our arrival, when we settled in, several hours later, maybe 9.00, 10.00, 11.00, we were in front of this hall, and all of a sudden there was some commotion. Everybody ran into the rooms, and those of us who were new there did the same. We entered Room 2 and they started shouting, "There's Duca." And this Duca appeared with another soldier, and they came straight to Room 2. There, they asked for a man whose identity card they had with them, and apparently they were looking for him. Allegedly he had raped some Serb woman, and allegedly they had found that identity card on that site. Then they beat him. When they were finished, they started beating another person, a person to whom they referred as a sniper. That took several minutes. Then they left the room. And then they took out prisoners from Room 3. Then they beat them outside, in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this person Duca to whom you've referred?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That too was a Serb soldier who often came to the camp, and each time when he came, there would be people beaten and killed. I mean, I didn't know him personally before. I met him there for the first time. Rather, I saw him there, not met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've referred to another person, another soldier, you said would come with him. Do you know the name of that other soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an inmate in the camp who was known as Singaporac?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Singaporac or the sniper. They called him sometimes this, sometimes the other. That man too was in Room number 2 with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: When I came to the camp, he was lying in a corner on pallets of some kind. We could only smell the stench coming from him. He hadn't moved for days. He was badly beaten up but still alive. On that first day when Duca appeared, he asked him -- that is, he demanded that the man stand up, but the man couldn't stand up. He couldn't move. Duca kicked him several times, and a day or two later, this man, Singaporac, died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to his body?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The corpse was removed and lay outside the building the whole day in the direction of Room number 3, where boxes of -- crates of bottles were standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, earlier you referred to some prisoners from Room 3 being beaten by this Duca person. Were any of the camp personnel present at that incident?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In that incident, while Duca was beating them, we were all locked up inside Room number 2 and we could only hear what was going on outside. And after Duca left, when the situation calmed down a little, of course we all went out. I saw other guards, including Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see Kajin doing and where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He was walking about among the prisoners. He was there a couple of minutes after Duca and the others left. The people from Room number 3 were still screaming with pain from the injuries they sustained, but he was outside with the other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that people were not specifically directed to attend -- to be housed in any particular room. What was the situation insofar as the rooms are concerned and the make-up of the people in each of the rooms?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In Room number 2, people were mostly from Prijedor, the majority of them, of course, from Puharska. In my room where I spent most of the time, in Room number 2, there were people from Kozarac, Kamicani, from Brdo, and in Room number 3, it was the same. And when later Room number 4 was open, the majority of detainees from Puharska and there were a couple of people from Ljubija. People from Ljubija were mainly in rooms number 4 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said earlier that the prisoners who were beaten were from Room number 3, the prisoners that Duca beat. My question is: Did you see Duca do anything else to those prisoners apart from beat them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He would pick two men each time and force them to beat each other. The detainees had to beat each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for clarity's sake, where were you when that took place?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I was in Room number 2, and all of that was happening outside Room number 2, between Room number 2 and Room number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see it, but we could hear it all because there were just a wall between us. It's just a matter of a couple of metres. We could hear everything. All the sounds came from the barred door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the camp, did a person by the name of Drago Tokmadzic become an inmate at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: During the first days after my arrival at the camp, Drago Tokmadzic would bring inmates. He was a policeman in Prijedor. At that time he was already working in Ljubija. And together with Esad Islamovic and on a daily basis or, rather, not every day, but he would bring inmates from Ljubija to Keraterm in his capacity as policeman. And one day the two of them came again together. We thought they had brought new inmates, but on that day was them who were brought as detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to Drago Tokmadzic and Esad Islamovic after they'd been brought to the camp as inmates?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether it was on the first or the second day after their arrival at the camp. They were placed into Room 4 and they were taken out one night. During that night, Drago Tokmadzic was killed. Esad was in a similar condition, but still he survived. Drago was killed that night, he succumbed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The same thing as before. I was listening the whole time to what was going on with them, how they were being beaten. I couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who beat them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The same as before. I could only judge by the voices. And it was not only me but the others as well who were in the vicinity and who were listening. We recognised Duca, Zigic, and Banovic. I assume another person was involved from Brdo, but I could not confirm this with any certainty, and nobody else could confirm it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated to the Court something about Duca. Do you know who this person Zigic was, and if so, how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: It's Zigic, actually. Zigic was a taxi driver in Prijedor, and I know him by sight. I didn't really know him personally or socialise with him, but I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the person Banovic you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The Banovics are twin brothers who worked there as guards. I can't say anything bad about one of the brothers, but as far as the other is concerned, my experiences are unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe just briefly what this other person, this one that you said was unpleasant, looked like?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He was small, short. He had longish hair. We called him Cupo because he was disheveled. He would always play with a knife, throw it into the air, and he would throw it at me. And one day he slapped me on the face just because I was wearing glasses which had darkened in the sun. He thought it was some kind of provocation, whereas I was simply wearing sun shades, and that was enough reason for him to slap me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you didn't see what happened but you could hear the voices. Did you hear those voices referring to each other by name, that is Duca, Ziga, Zigic and Banovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion, Mr. Tomic, when guards took inmates out of the camp for any specific purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of one time when they took out five to six inmates, volunteers, and went with them to some rooms opposite Keraterm. Those were some sort of warehouses. And for an entire day, they sort of carried some sort of stuff which was in that warehouse, and they worked there the whole day. And I know of another occasion when one of the inmates went home and was returned the same day. He had gone to see his family, to have a shower, and was returned on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just referring to the earlier occasion, how do you know what went on there? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred earlier to an occasion when some volunteers were taken out of the camp and had to look through some goods. How do you know what they had to do?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I know because among these people were some of my acquaintances, including my best man, Mirsad Radic, and he told me all about what they had done there. Also he brought a piece of carpeting from that warehouse on which he prayed every day for all those who had been killed at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what in particular these goods were?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Those were things which had been brought, stolen, from villages which had been torched, such as television sets, household appliances, furniture, tractors, and they sorted these things for an entire day, classified them sort of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they volunteered to do this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the most important reason for anyone to do any sort of work was their expectation that they would get something extra to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, were there any persons of Albanian ethnicity Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 detained in the camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to any of those? And if so -- any of those people? And if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: There were Albanians. Some of them I knew personally. Or rather, from the very beginning, one of those Albanians, by the name of Bedzeti, was taken out every day, and that night when Drago Tokmadzic was killed and when Esad was beaten up, this Bedzeti was called out again and another man, another Albanian, was called out. He was the proprietor of the pastry shop called the Zvjezdas and his nickname was Zvjezdas. They called out another two Albanians who were also taken out and beaten up. There was an underage boy by the name of Jusufi, 17 years old, and another was also a pastry shop owner, Fejzo Fejzulahu. As far as Jusufi is concerned, I later heard that he survived that particular incident but he didn't survive the next one. He was killed in Keraterm. While Fejzulahu did survive, went to Omarska, from Omarska he went to Manjaca, and he lives in Germany today. As for Bedzeti, I heard later that he was killed in Keraterm too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were there any persons, to your knowledge, of Serbian ethnicity detained in Keraterm camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of two persons. One was Jovan Radocaj, and another one whose name doesn't matter really. He was half Serb. His father was a Serb and his mother was Croatian, and he asked us not to mention that he was a Serb, and he was with us the whole time, and he got out of Keraterm, left for Omarska, and further on, to Manjaca -- and then on, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to Jovan Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Radocaj was called out one night and allegedly he was caught by mistake. And they asked who the hell had brought him to the camp, what kind of fool. And somebody unlocked the door, he was released, and while he was leaving, he only said, "It's all over," and they started beating him immediately outside the building, and he was killed that night, that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who was beating him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was beaten and killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Allegedly he had voted for the SDA at the elections, and there were those SDA posters in his house. Even I know that, because I used to see them while passing by his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, while you were detained in Keraterm camp, were you ever questioned or interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No. Not one of the detainees who were from Ljubija was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said earlier that you left Keraterm camp on July the 4th. Where did you go from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: From Keraterm, they transferred us to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "us," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to these people from Ljubija, this group of people who were not interrogated at Keraterm. And in fact, it was the explanation given. The day before, another list was made, including 115 names, and the next day we were supposed to be returned to Ljubija for interrogation. Because we were supposed to be returned to Ljubija for interrogation, two men from Prijedor managed to get their names on that list and left with us for Omarska, and then another three men from Kozarac, I believe. They had been caught somewhere on Mount Kozara and they were in Stara Gradiska prison, and together with us, they left for Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that you were supposed to be returned to Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I think -- I can't now -- I think it was one of those shift leaders, somebody with a higher rank. I wasn't present when this was announced. In any case, it was the same man, Anusic Nono, who made the list. Who instructed him to do it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for how long did you remain at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Omarska until the 6th of August, until the closure of the camp. When the people were divided, more than a half went to Manjaca, others went to Trnopolje, and less than 200 people were left at Omarska. So I left on the 6th of August for Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the prisoners treated in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In a beastly manner. No rules applied whatsoever. There was no human dignity at all. They killed us. They did whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything in particular happen to you while you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, daily beatings were so regular that they didn't even represent anything special any more. I was once beaten up so badly, I spend the next four days in a coma. I was thrown out onto a heap of corpses, and I was found there by one of my comrades who brought me back to the world of the living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to continue?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that was doing -- that beat you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: There were many, many of them. That night, the worst night I had there, the one who started was young Kvocka, and then another few men joined him, then another few, and finally there were eight of them beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this person Kvocka you're referring to, what position in the camp at Omarska did he occupy?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He was an ordinary guard. As far as I heard, he was a brother of one of the guard's commanders, Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general in Omarska, did the guards participate in beatings?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That was done on a daily basis, any time of day or night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about -- were there shift commanders in Omarska camp from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of those persons participate in beatings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: From what I knew, the shift leaders were Mladen Radic, called Krkan; a person called Ckalja; and Kvocka. I only know that Kvocka also was involved in killings, and I did not see the other two beating anyone in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what position did he occupy in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Kvocka. Kvocka was one of the leaders of the guard. He could also be seen with lists from which he would read out names of people, and he take people away and these people would not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, Mr. Tomic, were you aware of who the president of the Banja Luka municipality was?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: From television. I knew of him from the media. I think his name was Radic. Radic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see that person at Keraterm -- at Omarska camp? And if so, in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: In the middle of July -- at that time I was on the pista, the tarmac. And one day we were being prepared to sing songs because a delegation was to come from Banja Luka, and we were to welcome them with song and sort of in a dignified way. And so we were practising singing songs so that the next day when this delegation came in on helicopter, we sang Serb nationalist songs with our arms -- hands raised in a three-finger salute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that salute signify, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: It was -- it's always been the Serbian salute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many members of this delegation were there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know, six, seven, up to ten. They reviewed us and then they toured the camp. They went to certain buildings. Then they went to the administration building, and they spent about half an hour there, perhaps longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "they reviewed us"?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: They did not review us. They toured the rooms where we were, rooms where there were other prisoners who were detained, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, just before the camp closed, was there an occasion when some prisoners from Keraterm arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a day or two before I left Omarska, two buses arrived from Keraterm -- from Keraterm. That was two busloads. And among these people, I found Anto Gavranovic a colleague from Prijedor, and he told me that they were not interrogated there and they had been sent to Omarska to be interrogated. They also put them in various rooms, and then, late in the evening, they started collecting them again. They were reading their names off certain lists because allegedly they were going to go to be exchanged. And so this friend of mine also left. And no one knows what happened to them afterwards. In any event, they were brought in that day, and that same night they were taken out of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what became of them when they left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Later on, I met my colleague's brothers, and they asked me what happened -- what happened to him. And later on, I read in a Bosnian and Croatian newspapers, the media, that they were looking for him. In other words, they were -- members of those families were asking for their own. His name was appearing in the media. His brothers were looking for him. I don't know what happened. I did not know anyone else among those men, but I know that this person specifically has been sought, and he was never found. The last time I had any contact with his brothers was about three years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, were there any policemen from Ljubija in Omarska camp while you were there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: You mean as inmates or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As inmates, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a policeman who, after the takeover of power by Serbs, stayed on on duty as a policeman, but then he ended up in the camp, first at Keraterm and then we were together in Omarska, and his name was Ismet Taras.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if anything happened to him while he was in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: One night -- he was with me together on the tarmac area, and we were going to the restaurant to sleep at night. And one evening, this man Milan Anusic, another inmate, came. He called his name out several times, saying that Krkan wanted him. He did not respond. He was close to me, and he said something in a sense that he was finished. And only after two or three attempts on the part of Anusic to bring him out, Krkan appeared, and then he got up and left. And that was the last time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred earlier to killings that would take place in Omarska. What would become of the bodies of the persons who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: It depended on where they were killed. If they were killed in front of an area -- the wash area, that was a car wash area, that's where killings were taking place. Or they were dumped around the "white house" and the next -- the following day, in the morning, they would be loaded on a pickup truck and taken away. And every day, there were 10, 15 or more bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the day that this delegation visited Omarska camp, were there any bodies in the vicinity that was visited by the delegation, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The bodies were usually taken -- driven away in the morning, and there was a driver who would take them away. There was a man called Kovac who used to work for the mining company. I don't believe that the bodies were still around the "white house" when the delegation arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just pardon me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder whether the usher could just push the ELMO back, a little bit further back because my view of the witness is slightly obscured, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, please let me know if you want to stop at any time. I notice you became slightly overcome at one point, but just let me know if you want to stop, won't you, please? Thank you very much. Mr. Tomic, very briefly, after you had been in the various camps, did you at any stage serve in the HVO or the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer has come out as "yes," but I think it may have been "no," in fact. Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The answer was inaudible. The interpreter read off the lips. If you can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you give us the answer to the question, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you may need to come a little closer to the microphones, because you speak quietly and it's not picking you up, Mr. Tomic. Thank you very much. The question was this: After your stay in the various camps did you serve at any stage in the HVO or the Croatian military forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The period at the end of 1991/1992, it's right, isn't it - and I think you've told us this - that people started to refuse to answer their call-ups for military service? Was one of the consequences of that that the JNA effectively became denuded of people of Croatian or Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: It is not correct. There were still both Muslims and Croats in JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As time went on, did those who had answered their call-ups, did those people also begin to stop taking part in the Serb military forces or did the JNA remain a mixed force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: There were still Muslims and Croats in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that also true of the police who operated both in Prijedor and more particularly in Ljubija, that they remained a mixed force for quite a long time after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that remain the position until you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know the answer to this, help us, please: Did it remain the position for sometime after your detection that the police remained a mixed force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I can answer that question. I have mentioned already that the police commander in Ljubija throughout that period was a Croat. His name was Branko Bjekic. He was the commander of the Ljubija police until the end of July, and in late July he, too, was then brought to Omarska as an inmate, and that was the end of the mixed police, as far as I know in respect of Ljubija. After he -- after he had rounded up all men in Ljubija, then he, too, ended up in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as your own personal employment was concerned, Mr. Tomic, it's right that your work continued until May 1992, but after that, work dried up because the iron ore mine where you were working lacked orders or lacked work to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: These are economic matters. I don't know if there were orders. I don't know that. But be that as it may, the ore was not leaving the mine, so there was no need for us to come to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, just briefly, please, concerning this: Is it right that there came a time when the Territorial Defence, the TO, took up regular guard duties in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is the "regular" guards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I perhaps didn't phrase that terribly well. Did the TO take up guard duties in Ljubija at some stage before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that on a daily and nightly basis that the TO was patrolling?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was the TO still a mixed military unit in terms of ethnicity or had it become factionalised, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No. They were still mixed. The only problem was that they did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they didn't have weapons, are you talking about all forms of weapons or didn't have heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: They only had light weapons, the TO, but they had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to break in and say that might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this would be a convenient time. Mr. Tomic, we're going to take a break until ten minutes after 4.00, and during the break, you're not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including the members of the Prosecution team. The interpreter Mr. Pierre Rouve will you please attend on the Chamber in my room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, we will stop at about five minutes to 5.00 because there is a matter I have to raise with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm anticipating finishing well before then.
