utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you'll need your microphones on and you'll need to come a bit closer, please. Well done. If I can just briefly ask you one or two questions about the -- your arrest, Mr. Tomic? If you can confirm this, a total of, I think, 13 of you were arrested at the same time and taken to Keraterm at the same time, all men of military age, in other words, between 16 and 60? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived in the early hours of the 14th of June at Keraterm. Can you just tell us the time of your arrival, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: It could have been 5.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having arrived there and entered the premises, you were taken almost immediately, I think, to the main building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, and ask you about somebody called Zivko Knezevic, who had, I think, the nickname Ziza. Is that a name with which you're familiar, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Ziza?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ziza, I'm sorry, I'm being reminded to brush up on my pronunciation here on the right. Is that a name with which you're familiar, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a name I heard often at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this correct, that other inmates told you that that individual held high rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you were told by others at the camp that that individual was superior to the shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told anything specific as to what his duties were and what kind of assignments he gave, but in any case, he was occupying a high Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 position, at the camp, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- although you heard of him, did you know what this man looked like?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tomic, the people who were employed as guards at Keraterm, is this right, that you observed that they wore a variety of different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of which appeared to be police uniforms and others of which appeared to be military uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now just briefly to ask you about one or two individual incidents, if I may, please. The man called Singaporac, he had a nickname, Snajperista. Do you know how he acquired that nickname?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Allegedly, he got both of his nicknames from Duca but for what reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the incident involving this individual, was that on the first afternoon that you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any event, very soon after you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. Duca Knezevic, was it your observation that he was not a guard at the camp but someone who came in from outside?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He had arrived in a Mercedes into the compound together with another soldier, and he would come to the camp only occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you now, please, about a gentleman called Stipo Susic, who I believe was a Catholic priest interned at Keraterm? Do you recall him? Or Sosic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Sosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sosic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Stipo Sosic arrived on the same day as I did, but sometime during that day of the 14th of June, I remember we had a pack of cigarettes between us. We spent the night together in room number 4, and on the next day he was transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he of Croat ethnicity as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He was a Catholic priest. He worked in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if he survived his stay at Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He survived Keraterm, Omarska, Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other gentlemen in Keraterm who were either priests or Muslim Imams, hajjis that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I heard there had been another seven Muslim religious persons. I hadn't met them, but I heard they had been at that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two policemen, Drago Tokmadzic and Esad Islamovic, respectively a Croat and a Muslim by ethnicity, you actually saw those two individuals bringing prisoners to Keraterm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that continued pretty well up until the time they themselves were detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request, would the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, the interpreters are asking that you speak up, speak more clearly, more loudly. Perhaps you should come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's not easy if you have a quiet voice, Mr. Tomic, but you'll have to just remember, if you can, please, to keep your voice up. You also spoke of a Muslim policeman who was at Omarska. Did you ever see that individual bringing prisoners to either of the two camps?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't bring anyone to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he continued with his duties as a policeman up until the time that he was detained? Did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It's true that he performed his duties until his arrest. I still saw him in Ljubija after the takeover of power by Serbs. I know he was still working. I used to see him. He was wearing his uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you've told us about one Serbian person who was at Keraterm as a detainee, Jovan Radocaj. Were you aware of any other persons of Serb ethnicity who were being held at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I mentioned another one who was a half Serb. His father was a Serb and his mother was Croatian. He was with me at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what his name was, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be so kind as to tell us what it was, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Zelimir Komosar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at Keraterm, did you at any stage become aware that one of the detainees there was a military aviation pilot called Bajazit Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him by name. I only knew that he was a pilot, and he was also in room number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when that person eventually appeared to be suffering from mental problems of some sort whilst you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that person again at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally this, Mr. Tomic, please: You departed for Omarska on the 6th of -- I'm sorry. Some prisoners came from Keraterm to Omarska on the 6th of August. Did they come by bus, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Some detainees from Keraterm arrived at Omarska around the 6th of August. Did they arrive by bus, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th of August. They arrived in buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to assess the numbers of detainees arriving in that way?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I talked with this one man. He told me there were 180 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did they remain at Omarska before they were taken away again?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Only that day. During the night, they were called out again and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me a moment, please? Yes. I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to start, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. I am lawyer Goran Rodic from Podgorica. I wish to tell you straight away that I regret very much all that you have gone through, but you must understand that we too must do our job. You have said during your examination-in-chief that you opted in that period of 1991, 1992, when the elections were, for the reformist party which was then led, if I'm correct, by Ante Markovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everyone knows more or less that the policy of that party was based on an economic programme for the entire Yugoslavia; is that correct? Will you please answer audibly so that it can be reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, could you please tell me, was that party very different in many respects from the nationalist parties which had the upper hand after all in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The difference was enormous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, in your view, and bearing in mind all that has happened, could you please explain to the Honourable Court whether that difference was enormous in a positive or a negative sense compared to the nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Certainly in a positive sense, because the entire plan and the programme of that party was based on an economic programme, without much political influence, whereas nationalist parties were responsible for where we are today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. That's why I asked you this question. Since I'm aware that at the time there was a huge rally in support of Ante Markovic, president of that party, and did you attend that rally?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that the rally took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it widely attended?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the slogan of that rally was co-existence of all the people in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you have just said, and you assessed that it was the politics of those other parties which led us to the situation today, I remember that during your examination-in-chief, you stated your view on the issue of removal of people who were taken to Keraterm and Omarska. Can you tell us, in your view, who were the people who decided that these things were going to be done?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I can say that from my home town, Ljubija, those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 were the people who decided who would go to the camps, and they were from the leadership of the SDS, and leaders of the Crisis Staff, as they called themselves, in Ljubija. So the people in power in Ljubija at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about other areas in that region, who the people were who made those decisions?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, related to this, and I'm only asking for your opinion, the people who are sitting behind me now, and about whom this trial is, would you tell us, in your view, did they have any influence on the establishment and creation of the camps of Omarska and Keraterm? Did they have that sort of power?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I hadn't known those people before. I know them only from the camps. Whether they had influence, I don't know, but they did have influence at the camp, inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. They were the security there, but I was talking about the creation and incarceration of people in those camps.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had any other kind of influence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, since you also mentioned the curfew imposed after the takeover of power in Prijedor, you spoke about the peaceful walks, as you refer to them. Since you took those walks even after the curfew, did you suffer any consequences?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could we note that you were not in any physical danger as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that until the 24th of May, you worked in the iron ore mine, and you said this was your last working day. Could you tell me, when you were going to work, did you take the bus every day?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This road from your home to work, was it clear, the road that this bus took?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No audible answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, we didn't hear the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that until that day, there were no roadblocks on the road?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were talking about the TO, that is, the Territorial Defence, were you referring to the Territorial Defence unit for the Ljubija area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the local TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the Territorial Defence was stationed in the school building in Ljubija. Were all the members of that unit stationed at the school or was it just the command of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: All of them were locals from Ljubija, and they came there only when their shift was on duty, when they had particular assignments. That was it as far as the TO was concerned. That was all they did at that building. Beforehand, they used to have weapons which they returned, I mean the weapons they had been issued with, but in any case, they were left without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, those members of the TO, did they come to that school in their uniforms, without any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Wearing their uniforms, without weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe what they were doing, what their assignment was?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what their assignment was. At any rate, they had their wartime assignment, and it was such that they served in the TO or in the reserve units of the army or the reserve units of the police. That's where they were assigned as wartime assignments, where they were supposed to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, we could call it mobilisation of the reserve units of the TO, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you, too, put on your uniform and set out to go there.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did you have?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I had a uniform from the reserve forces of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you stated that in 1981 you served your regular military service in Belgrade, can you please tell me what was your branch of service? What is the kind of training that you had?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you completed your military service, you were transferred to the reserve force. Which unit? Which branch?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: The reserve force of the infantry. Right now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter if you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I can't really recall now the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. The person about whom you said that he headed the Crisis Staff in Ljubija, Slobodan Taranjac --

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Taranjac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, what he did before that situation in terms of occupation?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He worked at the Tomasica mine as a foreman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that man have a university degree or just secondary education?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: He had secondary education and perhaps completed some courses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about him even before those events in your hometown?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you mean whether I knew him? Yes. He was a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all these things began to happen in the area of Prijedor, did he take a much more visible position than before?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take up a more prominent position in society?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Among Serbs, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again in relation to him, were you ever told why you were being taken to Keraterm? Were you ever given a reason?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me. And even at the interrogation at Omarska, I was asked why I was at the camp. The inspector asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Milan Curguz, also known as Krivi.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, was he an active-duty policeman in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: No. He, too, was a reserve policeman before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's a member of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned seeing Curguz on several occasions when he brought some people to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the Ljubija area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do that on his own initiative or was it on somebody's orders that he escorted these people, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it was his own initiative. I assume it was on somebody's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, when you arrived at Keraterm, you said you first went to Room number 2?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me if you know the approximate number of people at that time in Room number 2?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Close to 400 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, where did you settle in when you arrived? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Right at the entrance to Room number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Milan Anusic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saying that he kept a list of prisoners who were inside Room number 2?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that list on him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, was anybody asked to volunteer to make a list of people in that room?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any deadline for making this list?

utterances.speaker: ANTE TOMIC
utterances.text: Anusic was given this notebook to make a list of all the people inside the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, as I indicated, we would stop at five minutes to 5.00 today. Mr. Tomic, we are now going to take the adjournment until 9.30 tomorrow morning. During the break, you're reminded that you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including the members of the Prosecution team. Would you escort the witness out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you remember that we had discussed the ways in which the translator, Mr. Pierre Rouve, would be assisting the Chamber. And one of the ways would be to have him translate before the witness summaries -- to translate into French the witness summaries. We understand that it would be virtually impossible for him to do that in a timely manner so that it would be ready for court, because the witness summaries are necessarily prepared rather late in time. But I was given to understand that a practical arrangement had been worked out whereby the Prosecutor would make available to him a draft, which, I understand, the OTP would have already - it's a draft of the summary - on the understanding, of course, that the summary in its final analysis would have adaptations to that draft. But that draft would be nonetheless helpful to the Chamber if we could have that translated. And if that's something the OTP already has, then that could be made available to the translator well in advance of the court proceedings and at a time that would be consistent with the professional requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour. The request for the summaries came a little bit late in the day, in the sense that we had prepared certainly our own method of examining witnesses and had statements, et cetera, but the actual summaries are being done evenings and weekends by the prosecutors as we go along. And we are trying to -- we are trying to get them in a timely manner and then use them for proofing sessions. I can tell you that some of them are ready and have been prepared in advance, but they have not all been prepared. And we certainly can provide those which have been prepared, almost immediately, but I cannot say that they have all been prepared for the balance of the witnesses. That's what we are using our evenings and weekends to do. So in so far as we can provide what we have, we will do that immediately, and as they are done we will provide a copy at your request, with the understanding that they are subject to amendment after the proofing session, because sometimes -- and we would then source them as we do, as you can see, that some paragraphs have "proofing session" behind them, meaning that there is additional information which was derived from that or amendments made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely my understanding. And if that could be done, that would be very helpful to the Chamber. So would you see that that is done?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We will attend to that immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may suggest something, because there is a proffer of the testimony that we have received almost on all the witnesses, which is basically the whole summary, just it's not being segmented in various paragraphs, and for those that those summaries are not being made, perhaps those proffers of testimony, it could be given and translated, if you have most of them. But I have received almost on all witnesses. So that could be also helpful, because you do have it on the file already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the same thing we are talking about, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I might say that in our attempt to provide full and thorough disclosure - and I don't think my friends will complain about our disclosure - we have provided them with documents that had been prepared a long time ago, even before the selection of the new witness list when Mr. Sikirica was added and we had to change the indictment. Needless to say, we have provided our friends with a document which was known as a proffer that was made perhaps years ago, but that is not the same as the witness summary. They are two totally different things. This is something that may not even amount to a statement. It may be internal and -- may be internal work product, in the sense that it may be an investigator's distillation of three or four statements that a witness may have made, as a suggestion as to what the witness might testify to down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. We will adhere to the procedure that we had worked out. Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. We will adjourn until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry, did Your Honour mean 9.30 or 9.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will be 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
